description: Lists, dicts, tuples, and sets — the containers that hold your data.

screens.body:
A list holds several values in order, inside square brackets. It's the container you'll reach for most — shopping lists, task lists, playlists.

Counting starts at 0, not 1. The first item is index 0, the second is index 1. This trips up everyone at first, then becomes second nature.
screens.heading: Lists: ordered collections
screens.keyPoint: Lists hold ordered items; counting starts at 0.

screens.body:
Lists can change after you make them. append() tacks an item onto the end. len() tells you how many items are inside.

There's also remove() to take an item out and pop() to grab-and-remove the last one — but append and len cover most days.
screens.heading: Changing lists
screens.keyPoint: append() adds to the end; len() counts items.

screens.body:
Slicing grabs a chunk of a list: list[start:end]. The start index is included, the end index is not — it stops one short.

Negative indexes count from the end: -1 is the last item. Handy when you want "the last three" without doing math.
screens.heading: Slicing
screens.keyPoint: [start:end] grabs up to — but not including — end.

screens.body:
A dict (dictionary) stores pairs: each key maps to a value, inside curly braces with colons. Think of it like a real dictionary — look up a word (the key), get its definition (the value).

You look things up with dict[key]. Keys are usually strings; values can be anything — numbers, strings, even lists.
screens.heading: Dicts: labeled storage
screens.keyPoint: Dicts map keys to values; look up with dict[key].

screens.body:
A tuple looks like a list but uses parentheses — and it can't be changed after creation. No append, no reassignment. It's locked.

Use tuples for data that shouldn't change: coordinates, RGB colors, a date of birth. The lock is a feature — it protects the data from accidental edits.

check.question: What happens if you try point[0] = 9?

screens.heading: Tuples: locked lists
screens.keyPoint: Tuples are like lists you can't edit — use ().

screens.body:
A set holds unique items only — duplicates are silently dropped. Order isn't guaranteed, so don't rely on positions.

Sets are perfect for "have I seen this before?" questions: unique visitors, tags on a post, usernames that must not repeat.
screens.heading: Sets: unique items only

screens.body:
Quick guide: need order and plan to edit? List. Need to look things up by name? Dict. Data that must never change? Tuple. Need uniqueness? Set.

They also nest — a dict can hold lists, a list can hold dicts. Real programs mix them constantly, like a student record with a name and a list of courses.

screens.heading: Picking the right container
screens.keyPoint: List for order, dict for lookup, tuple for fixed, set for unique.
